topics.h: Can one child clean a whole muddy path? Maybe not. But what about four children?
p: The lesson 'Together We Can' is about friends who do a big job by working as a team.
Teamwork means people work together to reach one goal.
When everyone does a small part, a big job becomes easy.
To answer a question about a story, find the line that gives the answer.
The title of a story often tells us its main idea.

ex.q: Read: The rain had washed mud all over the school path in Mysuru. "It is too much for me," sighed Meera. Then Arjun brought a broom, Salma brought a bucket and Tenzin brought a spade. Everyone took one small job. By lunch, the path was clean. "Alone we are small," smiled their teacher, "but together we can!" Question: How did the children clean the path so quickly?
st: Look for the line about the work: 'Everyone took one small job.'
So each child did one part of the work.
Many hands together finished the big job fast.
ex.a: They shared the work. Each child did one small job.

topics.rl: Cleaning the classroom, making a rangoli for a school festival or playing kabaddi: all of these need teamwork.

topics.h: 'Team' + 'work' makes 'teamwork'. Two small words can join to make a new one!
p: To cooperate means to work together and help each other.
Synonyms are words with the same or nearly the same meaning: help and assist.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings: together and alone, strong and weak.
A compound word is made of two smaller words: team + work = teamwork, class + mate = classmate.

ex.q: Think it through: what is the opposite of 'together' in this sentence? 'We cleaned the room together.'
st: 'Together' means with other people.
The opposite would be with no one else.
The word for that is 'alone': 'I cleaned the room alone.'
ex.a: alone

topics.rl: When your class plays tug of war, you cooperate with your classmates and pull together.

topics.t: Naming words: common, proper and collective nouns
topics.h: Meera, Mysuru, broom and team are all naming words. What kind of naming word is each?
p: A noun is a naming word. It names a person, place, animal or thing.
A common noun is a general name: girl, city, river, broom.
A proper noun is the special name of one person, place or thing: Meera, Mysuru, Ganga. It begins with a capital letter.
A collective noun names a group: a team of players, a flock of birds, a herd of elephants.
More groups: a swarm of bees, a bunch of grapes, a pack of wolves.

ex.q: Think it through: find the nouns in 'A team of girls from Pune won a cup.'
st: 'team' names a group, so it is a collective noun.
'girls' and 'cup' are general names, so they are common nouns.
'Pune' is the name of one particular city, so it is a proper noun.
ex.a: team (collective), girls and cup (common), Pune (proper)

topics.rl: Your school name, your city and your best friend's name are proper nouns. Your school's cricket team is a collective noun!

topics.h: Close your eyes. Tinkle! Ding-dong! Jingle! Can you hear the bells just from the words?
p: 'The Tinkling Bells' is a poem full of the sounds that bells make.
Sound words are words that sound like the noise they name: tinkle, buzz, hiss, splash.
Animals have sound words too: a cow moos, a duck quacks, a bee buzzes, an owl hoots.
Poets use sound words so that we can 'hear' the poem in our mind.
Sound words are often repeated: tick-tock, pitter-patter, ding-dong.

ex.q: Read this poem: Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell, / Ding-dong, ding-dong, the school bells tell. / Jingle, jingle, my ghungroos sing, / Clang, clang, the big brass bells ring! Question: Which sound word does the poet use for the cycle bell?
st: Find the line about the cycle bell: 'Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell'.
The word that copies the sound is 'tinkle'.
ex.a: tinkle

topics.rl: Listen at home: the pressure cooker whistles, the tap goes drip-drip and hot oil sizzles when puris go in.

topics.h: Bell, tell, shell, well... why do these words sound so good together?
p: Rhyming words end with the same sound: bell and tell, sing and ring.
Rhyming words do not need to start with the same letter: 'sing' and 'ring' still rhyme.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem. You can clap or tap along to it.
Each beat in a word is called a syllable. Clap 'jin-gle': 2 beats.
Repeating words like 'tinkle, tinkle' adds to the rhythm.

ex.q: Think it through: in 'Tinkle, tinkle, says my cycle bell, / Ding-dong, ding-dong, the school bells tell,' which words rhyme?
st: Look at the last word of each line: 'bell' and 'tell'.
Both end with the sound '-ell'.
So 'bell' and 'tell' rhyme.
ex.a: bell and tell

topics.rl: Many nursery rhymes and film songs use rhyme and a strong beat. That is why they are easy to remember!

topics.h: A bell, or a tiny, shiny, golden bell? Describing words make pictures in our mind!
p: An adjective is a describing word. It tells us more about a noun.
Adjectives can tell what kind (sweet, loud), what colour (golden), what size (tiny) or how many (two).
An adjective often comes before a noun: a shiny bell.
It can also come after 'is' or 'are': The bell is shiny.
Many adjectives have opposites: loud and soft, big and small, hot and cold.

ex.q: Think it through: find the adjectives in 'The tiny silver bell made a sweet sound.'
st: Ask: what kind of bell? 'tiny' and 'silver'.
Ask: what kind of sound? 'sweet'.
These three words describe nouns.
ex.a: tiny, silver, sweet

topics.rl: When you tell your friend about a 'big, red kite' or 'hot, crispy samosas', you are using adjectives.

topics.h: Superheroes are not the only ones who can stay safe. Smart children can too!
p: The lesson 'Be Smart, Be Safe' teaches us simple ways to keep ourselves safe.
On the road, cross at a zebra crossing. In India, look right, then left, then right again.
At home, never touch switches with wet hands, and stay away from a hot stove.
Your body belongs to you. If any touch makes you feel uncomfortable, say 'No' and tell a trusted adult.
A trusted adult is a grown-up who keeps you safe, like a parent, grandparent or teacher.

ex.q: Read: Kavya walked to school with her father. At the zebra crossing, they stopped. They looked right, then left, then right again. Only when the road was clear did they cross. "Safety first, always!" said Kavya with a smile. Question: What did Kavya and her father do before crossing?
st: Find the line just before they crossed.
'They looked right, then left, then right again.'
They crossed only when the road was clear.
ex.a: They stopped and looked right, left and right again, and crossed only when the road was clear.

topics.rl: Use these safety rules on your way to school, in the park and at home every single day.

topics.h: Not every stranger is bad, but smart children know the safety rules. Do you?
p: A stranger is a person you do not know.
Never go anywhere with a stranger, even if they offer sweets, toys or a ride.
Remember 'No, Go, Tell': say No loudly, Go away to a safe place, Tell a trusted adult.
Do not share your name, address, school or photos with people you meet online.
Learn a parent's phone number. In an emergency in India, an adult can call 112. The child helpline is 1098.

ex.q: Read: After school, Dev waited at the gate for his mother. A man he did not know said, "Your mother is busy. Come with me, I have chocolates." Dev said a loud "No!" He went back inside and told his teacher. His teacher called his mother, who came soon. Question: Did Dev do the right thing? Why?
st: The man was a stranger to Dev.
Dev said 'No' loudly, went back inside the school and told his teacher.
That is 'No, Go, Tell'.
ex.a: Yes. He said No, went to a safe place and told a trusted adult.

topics.rl: If you are ever lost in a market or mall, stay where you are, or ask a police officer or a shopkeeper at the counter for help.

topics.h: "Stop!" "Are you safe?" "What a busy road!" Every sentence has a different job.
p: A statement tells us something. It ends with a full stop (.): I walk to school.
A question asks something. It ends with a question mark (?): Where is your bag?
A command or request tells someone to do something. It ends with a full stop: Look both ways. Please close the door.
An exclamation shows a strong feeling like surprise or joy. It ends with an exclamation mark (!): What a big truck!
Every sentence begins with a capital letter.

ex.q: Think it through: what kind of sentence is 'Do not talk to strangers.'?
st: It does not just tell a fact, and it does not ask anything.
It tells someone what to do (or not do).
So it is a command. It ends with a full stop.
ex.a: A command

topics.rl: Safety signs use commands like 'Stop', 'Keep left' and 'Do not touch'.

topics.h: Can you colour a picture, watch cartoons and eat a samosa all at once? Things can get messy!
p: The poem 'One Thing at a Time' tells us to give our full attention to one task before we start the next.
To focus means to give all your attention to one thing.
When we focus, our work is neater and we finish it faster.
Things that pull our attention away, like a TV that is on, are called distractions.
The poem also says there is a time for work and a time for play.

ex.q: Read this poem: When I draw, I only draw, / I do not watch TV. / When I read, I only read, / The words come clear to me. / When work is done, I run to play, / And laugh the whole bright day! Question: What does the child do after the work is done?
st: Find the line that begins 'When work is done'.
It says 'I run to play'.
So the child plays only after finishing the work.
ex.a: The child runs out to play.

topics.rl: Switch off the TV while you do homework. You will finish quicker and have more time to play!

topics.t: Work and play: one and many
topics.h: One toy, two toys. One box, two... boxs? No! Let us find out the right way.
p: Work like homework and helping at home comes first. Play time is more fun when work is done.
To make most nouns plural (more than one), add -s: toy → toys, book → books.
Add -es to words ending in s, x, ch or sh: bus → buses, box → boxes, watch → watches, brush → brushes.
If a word ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: story → stories. But day → days, because 'a' comes before y.
Some words change in a special way: child → children, tooth → teeth, foot → feet, mouse → mice, leaf → leaves.

ex.q: Think it through: what is the plural of 'hobby'?
st: 'Hobby' ends in y.
The letter before y is 'b', a consonant.
So change y to i and add -es.
ex.a: hobbies

topics.rl: Count things in your room: two pencils, three boxes, four brushes. Saying them aloud is plural practice!

topics.t: Action words: verbs in the present
topics.h: Run, read, draw, jump! A sentence cannot work without an action word.
p: A verb is an action word. It tells what someone or something does: run, read, eat, sing.
We use the simple present tense for things we do every day: I play cricket every evening.
With I, you, we and they, the verb stays the same: I play, they play.
With he, she, it or one person's name, add -s: Asha plays. Add -es after s, x, ch, sh or o: watches, goes.
If a verb ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -es: fly → flies, cry → cries.

ex.q: Think it through: choose the right verb. 'Meena (read / reads) a story every night.'
st: Meena is one person, so she is like 'she'.
With she, we add -s to the verb.
So we write 'reads'.
ex.a: Meena reads a story every night.

topics.rl: Tell someone your daily routine: I wake up, I brush my teeth, I go to school. Those are present-tense verbs!

topics.h: Why would fast young deer need help from a slow old stag? Read on to find out!
p: 'The Old Stag' is a fable. A stag is a male deer.
A fable is a short story where animals talk and act like people. It teaches a lesson called a moral.
Every story has characters (who), a setting (where and when), a problem and a solution.
India has old collections of fables, like the Panchatantra and the Jataka tales.
To find the moral, ask: what did the characters learn at the end?

ex.q: Read this fable: In a forest near the Satpura hills lived an old stag named Dhruv. The young deer laughed, "You are so slow, grandpa!" One hot summer, the ponds dried up. The young deer were thirsty and worried. "Follow me," said Dhruv. He walked slowly to a hidden spring behind the big rocks. "I found it many summers ago," he said. The young deer said, "We are sorry. You are slow, but you are wise." Question: What lesson did the young deer learn?
st: At first, they laughed at Dhruv for being slow.
When there was no water, Dhruv's old memory saved them.
At the end they said, 'You are slow, but you are wise.'
ex.a: Old people may be slow, but they are wise because of their experience. We should respect them.

topics.rl: Your grandparents know old recipes, games and stories. Ask them. Their experience is a treasure!

topics.h: A stag, a doe and a fawn walk into a forest. Who is who?
p: Wisdom means good sense that comes from learning and experience.
A proverb is a short, wise saying: 'Look before you leap' means think carefully before you act.
'Slow and steady wins the race' means working steadily without giving up brings success.
Male and female names: stag – doe, lion – lioness, peacock – peahen, horse – mare, king – queen.
Young ones: deer – fawn, cat – kitten, dog – puppy, hen – chick, sheep – lamb, lion – cub.

ex.q: Think it through: what does 'Look before you leap' mean for Riya, who wants to jump into a puddle?
st: 'Leap' means jump.
'Look before you leap' tells us to check first.
Riya should check how deep or dirty the puddle is before jumping.
ex.a: Think and check carefully before you act.

topics.rl: Grandparents often use proverbs. Ask yours for a favourite one and what it means!

topics.t: Telling the past: past tense verbs
topics.h: Fables happened 'long, long ago'. So we tell them in the past tense!
p: The past tense tells us about something that has already happened: yesterday, last week, long ago.
Most verbs add -ed: walk → walked, laugh → laughed. If a verb ends in e, add -d: smile → smiled.
Some short verbs double the last letter: stop → stopped, hop → hopped.
If a verb ends in a consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed: cry → cried, dry → dried.
Some verbs change completely: go → went, see → saw, eat → ate, find → found, drink → drank, say → said.

ex.q: Think it through: change to the past: 'The old stag finds a spring.'
st: The verb is 'finds'.
'Find' does not take -ed. Its past form is special.
find → found
ex.a: The old stag found a spring.

topics.rl: When you tell your family about your day at school, you use the past tense: I played, I ate, I learnt.

topics.t: Louis Braille: the boy who made dots talk
topics.h: Can you read a book with your eyes closed? A teenage boy found a way!
p: The lesson 'Braille' tells the story of Louis Braille and his gift to the world.
Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. He lost his sight in an accident when he was a small child.
At his school in Paris, there were very few books that blind students could read.
As a teenager, he made a reading and writing system of raised dots. We call it braille.
World Braille Day is on 4 January, his birthday.

ex.q: Read: Louis Braille was born in France in 1809. When he was a small child, an accident hurt his eyes, and he lost his sight. At a school for blind children in Paris, he found very few books he could read. So, when he was only about fifteen, he made a new way of reading with raised dots. Today, people all over the world use braille. Question: Why did Louis Braille make a new way of reading?
st: Find the line about his school: 'he found very few books he could read.'
He wanted blind people to read easily.
So he made a system of raised dots.
ex.a: Because there were very few books that blind children like him could read.

topics.rl: Look out for braille dots on lift buttons, some medicine boxes and signs in railway stations and airports.

topics.h: Close your eyes and touch a coin. Can you feel its edges? Your fingers can 'see' too!
p: Braille is a code for reading and writing. It is not a separate language.
Each braille letter is made in a cell of 6 dot places: 2 columns of 3.
Different patterns of raised dots stand for different letters, numbers and marks.
The letter 'a' is just one raised dot at the top left of the cell.
Braille is read with the fingertips, moving from left to right. In India, Bharati Braille is used for Indian languages.

ex.q: Think it through: a braille cell has 2 columns with 3 dot places in each. How many dot places are there?
st: Each column has 3 dot places.
There are 2 columns.
ex.a: 6 dot places

topics.rl: People who are blind also use a white cane to find their way, and talking apps on phones that read text aloud.

topics.t: Everyone belongs: inclusion and word beginnings
topics.h: Ramps, braille signs and kind friends: they help everyone join in!
p: Inclusion means making sure everyone can take part, whatever their abilities.
Ramps, braille signs, talking books and sign language help people join in.
We use kind, respectful words. We say 'a person who is blind' or 'visually impaired'.
A prefix is added at the start of a word to change its meaning: un + kind = unkind.
un-, dis- and im- often mean 'not': unable, unfair, dislike, disagree, impossible, impolite.

ex.q: Think it through: Louis Braille showed that reading without sight was not im___. Which word fits?
st: 'Possible' means it can happen.
The prefix 'im-' means 'not'.
So 'impossible' means it cannot happen. Louis showed it was possible!
ex.a: impossible

topics.rl: In your class, you can include everyone: pick a new friend for your team, or help a classmate read the board.

topics.ch: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
topics.h: Can you stand like a mountain and balance like a tree? Yoga lets you try!
p: The lesson 'Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation' says that fit, healthy people make a strong country.
Being fit means having a strong, healthy body and a calm, happy mind.
Running, skipping, cycling, swimming and outdoor games keep us fit.
Yoga is an old Indian practice of body poses (asanas), slow breathing and relaxing.
International Day of Yoga is celebrated every year on 21 June.

ex.q: Read: Every morning, Anaya and her grandfather do yoga on the terrace in Pune. First they stand tall like a mountain in Tadasana. Then they balance on one leg like a tree in Vrikshasana. They breathe in slowly and breathe out slowly. "Now my body feels strong and my mind feels calm," says Anaya. Question: How does yoga help Anaya?
st: Find what Anaya says at the end.
'Now my body feels strong and my mind feels calm.'
So yoga helps both her body and her mind.
ex.a: It makes her body feel strong and her mind feel calm.

topics.rl: Try stretching for a few minutes every morning with a grown-up. Learn new poses only from a teacher or an adult who knows yoga.

topics.ch: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
topics.h: A habit is something you do again and again. Is your habit helpful or harmful?
p: Healthy habits: eat fruits and vegetables, drink clean water, sleep on time and play outdoors.
Wash your hands with soap before eating, and brush your teeth twice a day.
Too much junk food and screen time are not good for us.
The suffix '-ful' means 'full of': help + ful = helpful, care + ful = careful.
The suffix '-less' means 'without': care + less = careless, harm + less = harmless.

ex.q: Think it through: 'Eating only junk food every day can be ___ for your body.' Is it 'harmful' or 'harmless'?
st: 'Harmful' means full of harm. 'Harmless' means without harm.
Too much junk food is bad for the body.
So the right word is 'harmful'.
ex.a: harmful

topics.rl: Make a habit chart at home. Tick it each day you drink enough water, play outside and sleep on time.

topics.ch: Fit Body, Fit Mind, Fit Nation
topics.h: Do you breathe quickly or slowly in yoga? The answer is an adverb!
p: An adverb tells us more about a verb (an action word).
Some adverbs tell HOW: slowly, quickly, gently, loudly, carefully.
Some adverbs tell WHEN: today, now, early, tomorrow. Some tell WHERE: outside, here, there.
Many 'how' adverbs are made by adding -ly to an adjective: slow → slowly, quick → quickly.
If the word ends in y, change y to i: happy → happily, easy → easily.

ex.q: Think it through: find the adverb in 'Anaya breathes slowly.'
st: The verb is 'breathes'.
Ask: how does she breathe? Slowly.
'Slowly' tells us more about the verb, so it is an adverb.
ex.a: slowly

topics.rl: Your PE teacher says 'run quickly', 'stretch slowly' and 'land softly'. Those are adverbs!

topics.h: All you need is a ball, some flat stones and your friends. Ready for lagori?
p: 'The Lagori Champions' is about children who play lagori, a traditional Indian game.
Lagori is played with a ball and a pile of flat stones.
It has other names too. In many places it is called pitthu.
Two teams play. One team knocks down the pile with the ball and tries to build it again. The other team tries to get them out with the ball.
Lagori needs good aim, quick feet and teamwork.

ex.q: Read: It was the inter-school lagori match in Hubballi. Team Sunflower threw the ball and knocked down the pile of seven flat stones. Quickly, they began to stack the stones again. Team Mango tried to get them out with the ball. Just in time, Leela placed the last stone and shouted, "Lagori!" Team Sunflower won. Team Mango clapped and said, "Well played!" Question: How did Team Sunflower win?
st: Team Sunflower knocked down the pile.
They stacked the stones again while Team Mango tried to get them out.
Leela placed the last stone just in time and shouted 'Lagori!'
ex.a: They rebuilt the pile of stones before Team Mango could get them out.

topics.rl: Ask your parents or grandparents which games they played as children: gilli-danda, kho-kho, kabaddi or lagori?

topics.h: Team Mango lost, but they still clapped. Why do you think they did that?
p: A good sport plays fair and follows the rules.
A good sport is kind whether they win or lose. They say 'Well played!' to the other team.
A good sport helps a player who falls and respects the umpire or referee.
Useful words: opponent (the team you play against), captain (team leader), champion (winner), cheer (shout to encourage).
Opposites: win – lose, fair – unfair, start – finish.

ex.q: Think it through: Team Mango lost the match but clapped and said 'Well played!' What does this show?
st: Losing can make you feel sad.
Even so, they praised the winners.
Being kind to the other team after losing is sportsmanship.
ex.a: It shows good sportsmanship.

topics.rl: In school sports day, cheer for every runner, not just your friends. Shake hands after a match.

topics.h: Leela placed the stone. Leela shouted. Can one little word join these sentences?
p: A conjunction is a joining word. It joins words or sentences.
'and' adds things together: I like kabaddi and kho-kho.
'but' shows something different or surprising: We were tired, but we kept playing.
'or' gives a choice: Do you want a ball or a bat?
'because' gives a reason, and 'so' gives a result: We won because we worked together. It was dark, so we went home.

ex.q: Think it through: join 'Leela placed the last stone.' and 'Leela shouted "Lagori!"'
st: Both sentences tell what Leela did, one after another.
We are adding one action to another.
So we use 'and'.
ex.a: Leela placed the last stone and shouted "Lagori!"

topics.rl: You use conjunctions all the time: 'Can I go out and play? I finished my homework, so I am free!'

topics.t: Reading: a quiet morning in nature
topics.h: Sit still for one minute outside. How many living things can you spot?
p: 'Hekko' is a lesson set in nature. It invites us to look closely at the world around us.
Nature includes plants, animals, birds, insects, rain, soil and sky.
When we are quiet and patient, we notice small things, like ants or a snail.
Writers use our senses to describe nature: what we see, hear, smell and feel.
To answer a question about a passage, find the exact line that has the answer.

ex.q: Read: Early one morning, Tara sat quietly under a neem tree in her village in Odisha. She watched a line of ants carrying tiny crumbs. She heard a bulbul singing on a branch. She smelt the wet earth after the rain. A small snail was moving slowly on a leaf. "If I sit still and look closely," Tara thought, "nature shows me so much!" Question: Which things did Tara notice by seeing?
st: Look for the words 'watched' and things she saw.
She watched the ants carrying crumbs.
She also saw the snail moving on a leaf.
ex.a: The ants carrying crumbs and the snail on a leaf.

topics.rl: Keep a nature diary. Each day, write one thing you saw, heard or smelt outside.

topics.t: Looking closely: sense words and sound-alike words
topics.h: You can 'see' the sea and 'hear' a bird right here. Wait, what?
p: Observation means looking, listening and noticing carefully.
We use five senses: see (eyes), hear (ears), smell (nose), taste (tongue) and touch (skin).
Touch words: rough, smooth, prickly. Taste words: sweet, sour, salty, bitter.
A magnifying glass helps us observe tiny details, like the veins on a leaf.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: see – sea, hear – here, sun – son, flour – flower.

ex.q: Think it through: 'We went to ___ the ___.' Which pair goes in: see or sea?
st: 'See' means to look with your eyes.
'Sea' is a big body of salty water.
We go to look at the water, so: We went to see the sea.
ex.a: We went to see the sea.

topics.rl: On a walk, play 'I spy' with your family. It trains you to observe!

topics.h: The snail is ON the leaf. The ant is UNDER the stone. Little words tell us where things are!
p: A preposition tells us where something is, or its position.
Common prepositions: in, on, under, behind, between, above, near, in front of.
'in' means inside: The fish is in the pond. 'on' means on top of: The snail is on the leaf.
'between' means in the middle of two things: B comes between A and C.
'above' means higher than: The kite is above the trees.

ex.q: Think it through: 'Tara sat ___ the neem tree.' Which preposition fits: under, between or into?
st: Tara is below the branches of the tree.
'Between' needs two things, and 'into' shows going inside.
'Under' shows she is below the tree.
ex.a: Tara sat under the neem tree.

topics.rl: When you help find Dadi's glasses, you use prepositions: 'They are on the table, behind the radio!'

topics.t: Reading a poem about a swing
topics.h: Whoosh! Forward and back, up and down. What does it feel like to fly on a swing?
p: 'The Swing' is a poem about the joy of swinging high in the air.
A poem is written in lines. A group of lines is called a stanza.
Poems often have rhyming words at the ends of lines.
The person who writes a poem is called a poet.
Poets help us imagine: a swing can make us feel like we are flying.

ex.q: Read this poem: Under the banyan, my swing hangs low, / Didi gives a push and away I go! / Forward I fly with my toes to the sun, / Back I come laughing, oh, what fun! / The parrots cheer and the breezes sing, / My heart flies high on my happy swing! Question: Which words rhyme with 'go', 'sun' and 'swing'?
st: Look at the last word of each pair of lines.
low – go, sun – fun, sing – swing.
So 'low' rhymes with 'go', 'fun' with 'sun' and 'sing' with 'swing'.
ex.a: low, fun and sing

topics.rl: Next time you are on a swing in the park, say a rhyme to the beat of your swing!

topics.t: The joy of play: feeling words and opposites
topics.h: Up, down, forward, back! A swing is full of opposites, and full of joy!
p: Play makes us happy and healthy and helps us make friends.
Feeling words: happy, joyful, cheerful, excited, thrilled. Thrilled means very happy and excited.
Unhappy feeling words: sad, bored, upset, gloomy.
A swing shows many opposites: up – down, high – low, forward – backward, push – pull.
When we take turns on the swing, everyone gets to play.

ex.q: Think it through: 'Riya could not wait for her turn on the swing.' Which feeling word fits Riya: excited or bored?
st: 'Could not wait' means she really wanted her turn.
A bored person does not care.
So Riya is excited.
ex.a: excited

topics.rl: At the park, count how many children are waiting. Taking turns makes play fun for all.

topics.t: Words that take a noun's place: pronouns
topics.h: 'Didi pushed Didi's swing and Didi laughed.' Too many Didis! Let us fix it.
p: A pronoun takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it.
Didi → she, Arjun → he, the swing → it, Riya and I → we, the children → they.
Before the verb (doing the action) we use: I, you, he, she, it, we, they.
After the verb or after words like 'to' and 'with' we use: me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
The pronoun 'I' is always written as a capital letter.

ex.q: Think it through: replace the repeated nouns: 'Didi pushed Didi's swing and Didi laughed.'
st: Didi is a girl, so we use 'she' for the one doing the action.
For something that belongs to her, we use 'her'.
Didi pushed her swing and she laughed.
ex.a: Didi pushed her swing and she laughed.

topics.rl: When you talk about your friends, you use pronouns all the time: 'She is my best friend. We play together.'

topics.ch: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
topics.h: Tunnels, bridges and snowy peaks! Shall we hop on a little mountain train?
p: 'A Journey to the Magical Mountains' is a travel story about a trip to the mountains.
A travel story tells us where people went, how they travelled and what they saw.
Writers use describing words to help us picture places: snowy peaks, tall pine trees.
Mountains are often cold, especially at night and in winter.
The words 'first', 'then', 'far away' and 'that night' help us follow the journey.

ex.q: Read: In May, Ishaan's family took the toy train from Kalka to Shimla. The little train puffed through tunnels and over bridges. Pine trees stood tall on the slopes. Far away, Ishaan saw snowy peaks shining in the sun. "The mountains look magical!" he gasped. That night, it was so cold that he slept under two warm quilts. Question: How did Ishaan travel, and what did he see?
st: Find how they travelled: 'took the toy train from Kalka to Shimla'.
Find what he saw: tunnels, bridges, pine trees and snowy peaks.
Put the two answers together.
ex.a: He travelled by toy train and saw tunnels, bridges, pine trees and snowy peaks.

topics.rl: When you go on a trip, write a short travel diary: where you went, how you went and the best thing you saw.

topics.ch: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
topics.h: Peaks, valleys, glaciers and plateaus: Earth has so many shapes of land!
p: A mountain is very high land. Its top is called the peak, and its sides are slopes.
A valley is low land between hills or mountains. Rivers often flow through valleys.
A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly.
A plateau is high, flat land. A plain is wide, flat, low land. An island is land with water all around it.
The Himalayas are in the north of India. Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, is in the Himalayas.

ex.q: Think it through: Ishaan stands on a mountain and looks down at a low area with a river between two mountains. What is it called?
st: It is low land.
It lies between mountains.
Low land between hills or mountains is a valley.
ex.a: A valley

topics.rl: India has every kind of land: the Himalayas, the Ganga plains, the Thar Desert, the Deccan Plateau and islands like the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

topics.ch: A Journey to the Magical Mountains
topics.h: A hill is high. A mountain is higher. Mount Everest is the highest! How do words change when we compare?
p: To compare two things, add -er and use 'than': This hill is taller than that hill.
To compare three or more, use 'the' and add -est: Everest is the tallest of all.
Short words ending in one vowel + consonant double the last letter: big → bigger → biggest.
Words ending in y change y to i: happy → happier → happiest.
Long words use more and most: beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful. Special ones: good → better → best, bad → worse → worst.

ex.q: Think it through: 'Of all the peaks, Everest is the ___.' (high)
st: We are comparing many peaks, not just two.
So we use 'the' and add -est.
high → highest
ex.a: Of all the peaks, Everest is the highest.

topics.rl: You compare every day: 'My brother is taller than me. Mango is the best fruit!'

topics.h: Stone steps, a river, an old fort and the clack-clack of looms. Welcome to Maheshwar!
p: The lesson 'Maheshwar' takes us to a town of rivers, forts and weaving.
Maheshwar is a town in Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the river Narmada.
Ghats are wide steps that lead down to a river.
Rani Ahilyabai Holkar, a queen of the Holkar family, made Maheshwar her capital more than 250 years ago. The Ahilya Fort stands above the ghats.
The Narmada flows towards the west and falls into the Arabian Sea.

ex.q: Read: Maheshwar is a small town in Madhya Pradesh, on the banks of the river Narmada. Long stone steps called ghats lead down to the water. Above the ghats stands the old Ahilya Fort. In many homes, you can hear the clack-clack of handlooms. Weavers make the famous Maheshwari sarees there, thread by thread. Question: Name two things you can see near the river in Maheshwar.
st: Find the lines about the river.
'Long stone steps called ghats lead down to the water.'
'Above the ghats stands the old Ahilya Fort.'
ex.a: The ghats and the Ahilya Fort.

topics.rl: Many Indian towns grew up on river banks, like Varanasi on the Ganga and Maheshwar on the Narmada.

topics.h: Thread by thread, row by row, a beautiful saree grows on the loom!
p: A handloom is a loom worked by the weaver's hands and feet, without electricity.
The long threads on a loom are the warp. The threads that go across are the weft.
A shuttle carries the weft thread across the loom.
Maheshwari sarees are light sarees of cotton and silk. They are known for a border that can be worn on either side.
Heritage means the buildings, crafts, songs and ways of life from the past that we value and pass on. National Handloom Day is on 7 August.

ex.q: Think it through: why is weaving in Maheshwar called 'heritage'?
st: Weavers have woven sarees there for a very long time.
The skill is passed down from older weavers to younger ones.
Things from the past that we value and pass on are our heritage.
ex.a: Because it is an old craft that people value and pass on from one generation to the next.

topics.rl: Ask at home: is there an old saree, shawl or dhoti in your family that was woven by hand? That is heritage in your cupboard!

topics.h: maheshwar or Maheshwar? narmada or Narmada? Capital letters help special names stand tall!
p: Start every sentence with a capital letter.
Names of people, places, rivers, days and months begin with a capital letter: Ahilyabai, Maheshwar, Narmada, Monday, August.
The word 'I' is always a capital letter.
Names of seasons (winter, monsoon) do not need a capital letter unless they start a sentence.
Use commas to separate things in a list: We saw ghats, a fort and a loom. Also use a comma after 'Yes' or 'No' at the start: Yes, I can.

ex.q: Think it through: correct this sentence: 'in august, meena saw cotton silk and gold thread in maheshwar.'
st: Start the sentence with a capital: In.
Names of months, people and places need capitals: August, Meena, Maheshwar.
Put a comma between list items: cotton, silk and gold thread.
ex.a: In August, Meena saw cotton, silk and gold thread in Maheshwar.

topics.rl: When you write your address on a letter or a parcel, the names of your street, city and state all need capital letters.

qa.q: Story line: "Arjun brought a broom, Salma brought a bucket and Tenzin brought a spade." What did Salma bring?
qa.e: The line says 'Salma brought a bucket'.

qa.q: Story line: "The rain had washed mud all over the school path." What made the path dirty?
qa.e: The rain washed mud onto the path.

qa.q: Meera sighed, "It is too much for me." How did Meera feel at first?
qa.a: Worried that the job was too big
qa.e: 'It is too much for me' and a sigh show she felt the job was too big for one person.

qa.q: Story line: "By lunch, the path was clean." When was the path clean?
qa.e: The story says the path was clean by lunch.

qa.q: The teacher says, "Alone we are small, but together we can!" What does she mean?
qa.a: We can do big jobs when we work together
qa.e: The teacher means that a group working together can do what one person cannot.

qa.q: In "Everyone took one small job," which word tells us that all the children helped?
qa.e: 'Everyone' means all the people, so all the children helped.

qa.q: Which is the best title for the story about the muddy school path?
qa.e: The story is about friends cleaning the path together, so this title tells the main idea.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of teamwork?
qa.a: Four friends carry a heavy bench together
qa.e: Carrying a bench together means people are working as a team.

qa.q: What does 'cooperate' mean?
qa.e: To cooperate is to work together and help each other.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'help'?
qa.e: 'Assist' is a synonym of 'help'.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'together'?
qa.e: 'Together' means with others; 'alone' means with no one.

qa.q: Which two words join to make 'teamwork'?
qa.e: teamwork = team + work.

qa.q: Which of these is a compound word?
qa.e: classmate = class + mate, two smaller words joined together.

qa.q: Choose the right word: "Riya and Kabir ___ their crayons, so both can colour."
qa.e: When they share, both children can use the crayons.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'strong'?
qa.e: 'Weak' is the opposite of 'strong'. The other words mean almost the same as strong.

qa.q: "A big job becomes easy when many people help." Which word is the opposite of 'easy'?
qa.e: 'Difficult' means hard, the opposite of easy.

qa.q: Which of these is a proper noun?
qa.e: Chennai is the name of one particular city, so it is a proper noun.

qa.q: Fill in: "A ___ of bees buzzed near the flowers."
qa.e: A group of bees is called a swarm.

qa.q: Which word is a collective noun?
qa.e: 'Team' names a group of players, so it is a collective noun.

qa.q: In "Kabir lives in Shimla," which words are proper nouns?
qa.e: Kabir is a person's name and Shimla is a place's name. Both are proper nouns.

qa.q: Fill in: "A ___ of elephants crossed the river."
qa.e: A group of elephants is a herd.

qa.q: In "my cousin lives in agra.", which word is a proper noun that needs a capital letter?
qa.e: Agra is the name of a particular city, so it is a proper noun and needs a capital A.

qa.q: Which of these is a common noun?
qa.e: 'Mango' is a general name for a fruit. The others are special names.

qa.q: In "a team of players", what does the word 'team' name?
qa.e: 'Team' is a collective noun. It names a group.

qa.q: Which of these is a sound word?
qa.e: 'Buzz' sounds like the noise a bee makes.

qa.q: Poem line: "Clang, clang, the big brass bells ring!" Which word is the sound word?
qa.e: 'Clang' copies the loud sound of a big bell.

qa.q: What sound does a snake make?
qa.e: A snake makes a hissing sound: hiss!

qa.q: Which sound word fits light rain falling on a roof?
qa.e: Pitter-patter is the soft, quick sound of raindrops.

qa.q: Poem line: "Jingle, jingle, my ghungroos sing." What makes the jingle sound?
qa.e: The line says the ghungroos sing 'jingle, jingle'.

qa.q: Which animal says 'quack'?
qa.e: A duck quacks.

qa.q: Hot oil when puris go into the kadhai makes which sound?
qa.e: Hot oil sizzles when something is put in it.

qa.q: Fill in: "A stone fell into the pond with a ___."
qa.e: A stone falling into water makes a splash.

qa.q: Which word rhymes with 'bell'?
qa.e: 'Shell' ends with the same '-ell' sound as 'bell'.

qa.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
qa.e: 'Sing' and 'ring' both end with '-ing'.

qa.q: Clap the word 'tinkle'. How many beats does it have?
qa.e: tin-kle: 2 claps, so 2 beats.

qa.q: Clap the word 'butterfly'. How many beats does it have?
qa.e: but-ter-fly: 3 claps, so 3 beats.

qa.q: Which word rhymes with 'neck'?
qa.e: 'Neck' and 'check' both end with '-eck'.

qa.q: What is the rhythm of a poem?
qa.a: The beat you can clap to
qa.e: Rhythm is the beat of a poem.

qa.q: Which word does NOT rhyme with 'play'?
qa.e: 'Plan' ends in '-an'. The others end in '-ay'.

qa.q: Why does a poet write "Jingle, jingle" twice in one line?
qa.a: To make a sound and a beat
qa.e: Repeating the sound word makes us hear the bells and adds to the rhythm.

qa.q: Which word is an adjective in "The loud bell woke the baby"?
qa.e: 'Loud' describes the bell, so it is an adjective.

qa.q: "Grandma wore three green bangles." Which word tells how many?
qa.e: 'Three' tells us the number of bangles.

qa.q: Which adjective is the opposite of 'loud'?
qa.e: A loud sound is the opposite of a soft sound.

qa.q: Which word best describes the taste of a lemon?
qa.e: A lemon tastes sour. 'Sour' is an adjective.

qa.q: Which sentence has an adjective in it?
qa.e: 'Juicy' describes the mango.

qa.q: "The bell is shiny." Which word describes the bell?
qa.e: 'Shiny' tells us what the bell is like.

qa.q: Fill in: "Ice cream is ___."
qa.e: Ice cream is cold.

qa.q: Which word is NOT an adjective?
qa.e: 'Jump' is an action word (verb). The others describe nouns.

qa.q: Story line: "At the zebra crossing, they stopped." Where did Kavya and her father stop?
qa.e: The line says they stopped at the zebra crossing.

qa.q: Story line: "Only when the road was clear did they cross." When did they cross?
qa.e: They waited until no vehicles were coming.

qa.q: Kavya said, "Safety first, always!" What does she mean?
qa.a: Being safe is the most important thing
qa.e: 'Safety first' means we should think about being safe before anything else.

qa.q: Which is the safe way to cross a road in India?
qa.a: Look right, left, then right again
qa.e: In India vehicles drive on the left, so traffic near you comes from the right first.

qa.q: Which of these is a safe habit at home?
qa.a: Drying your hands before touching a switch
qa.e: Dry hands keep us safe from electric shock.

qa.q: Who is a trusted adult?
qa.e: A trusted adult is someone you know well who keeps you safe.

qa.q: A touch makes Riya feel uncomfortable. What should she do?
qa.a: Say 'No' and tell a trusted adult
qa.e: Riya should say no and tell a trusted adult. It is never the child's fault.

qa.q: Which word in "Be smart, be safe" means 'clever'?
qa.e: 'Smart' means clever or wise.

qa.q: What is a stranger?
qa.a: A person you do not know
qa.e: A stranger is someone you do not know.

qa.q: Story line: "Come with me, I have chocolates." What did Dev say?
qa.e: Dev said a loud 'No!' to the stranger.

qa.q: After saying no, where did Dev go?
qa.e: Dev went back inside, which was a safe place.

qa.q: Whom did Dev tell about the stranger?
qa.e: Dev told his teacher, a trusted adult.

qa.q: What do the words 'No, Go, Tell' remind us to do?
qa.a: Say no, go to a safe place, tell a trusted adult
qa.e: These three steps keep us safe from strangers.

qa.q: Someone you met in an online game asks for your home address. What should you do?
qa.a: Not share it and tell a parent
qa.e: We never share personal details online. Tell a parent or a trusted adult.

qa.q: What is the child helpline number in India?
qa.e: 1098 is the child helpline number in India.

qa.q: You are lost in a big market. Who is a good person to ask for help?
qa.e: A police officer is there to help people who are lost.

qa.q: Which sentence is a question?
qa.e: It asks something and ends with a question mark.

qa.q: What kind of sentence is "Look both ways before you cross."?
qa.e: It tells someone what to do, so it is a command.

qa.q: Which mark should end this sentence: "What a beautiful kite"
qa.e: It shows a strong feeling, so it ends with an exclamation mark.

qa.q: Which sentence is a statement?
qa.e: It tells us a fact and ends with a full stop.

qa.q: Which sentence is written correctly?
qa.e: It starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark.

qa.q: What kind of sentence is "Please hold my hand."?
qa.e: It asks someone politely to do something. A polite command is a request.

qa.q: Which sentence shows surprise?
qa.e: 'Wow' and the exclamation mark show surprise.

qa.q: Which mark ends a question?
qa.e: A question ends with a question mark (?).

qa.q: Poem lines: "When I draw, I only draw, / I do not watch TV." What does the child do while drawing?
qa.e: The child says 'I only draw' and does not watch TV.

qa.q: Poem lines: "When I read, I only read, / The words come clear to me." Why are the words clear?
qa.a: The child reads with full attention
qa.e: Reading with full focus helps the child understand the words.

qa.q: Poem line: "When work is done, I run to play." When does the child play?
qa.e: The child plays only after the work is finished.

qa.q: Which pair of words rhymes in the poem?
qa.e: 'Play' and 'day' end with the same '-ay' sound.

qa.q: What does 'focus' mean?
qa.a: To give full attention to one thing
qa.e: When you focus, all your attention is on one thing.

qa.q: Which child is focusing on the work?
qa.a: Asha does her sums with the TV off
qa.e: Asha has no distraction, so she can give full attention to her sums.

qa.q: What is the main message of the poem?
qa.a: Do one thing at a time with full attention
qa.e: The poem says to focus on one task and to play after work.

qa.q: Poem line: "And laugh the whole bright day!" How does the child feel?
qa.e: Laughing shows the child is happy.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'box'?
qa.e: Words ending in x take -es: boxes.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'story'?
qa.e: Story ends in a consonant + y, so y changes to i and we add -es.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'child'?
qa.e: 'Child' has a special plural: children.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'leaf'?
qa.e: In 'leaf', f changes to v and we add -es: leaves.

qa.q: Fill in: "Ravi packed three ___ into his school bag."
qa.e: Three means more than one, so we add -s: books.

qa.q: What is the plural of 'brush'?
qa.e: Words ending in sh take -es: brushes.

qa.q: Which of these is a chore (work) you can do at home?
qa.e: Folding clothes is a job that helps at home. The others are games.

qa.q: "Finish your homework first, then go out to play." Why is this a good plan?
qa.a: You can play freely with no work left
qa.e: When the work is finished, you can enjoy playing without worry.

qa.q: Which word is a verb?
qa.e: 'Write' is an action word.

qa.q: Fill in: "My brother ___ to school by bus."
qa.e: With one person (he), 'go' becomes 'goes'.

qa.q: Fill in: "The baby ___ when she is hungry."
qa.e: Cry ends in a consonant + y, so it becomes cries.

qa.q: Fill in: "We ___ our homework after lunch."
qa.e: With 'we', the verb stays the same: do.

qa.q: Fill in: "Asha ___ her hands before eating."
qa.e: Wash ends in sh, so with 'she' it becomes washes.

qa.q: Find the verb in "Kabir paints a big kite."
qa.e: 'Paints' tells what Kabir does.

qa.q: Fill in: "The cat ___ milk."
qa.e: The cat is 'it', so we add -s: drinks.

qa.q: Fill in: "Rohan and Meera ___ chess on Sundays."
qa.e: Rohan and Meera are two people (they), so the verb stays 'play'.

qa.q: Story line: "In a forest near the Satpura hills lived an old stag named Dhruv." Where did Dhruv live?
qa.a: In a forest near the Satpura hills
qa.e: The first line tells us the setting: a forest near the Satpura hills.

qa.q: The young deer laughed, "You are so slow, grandpa!" Why did they laugh at Dhruv?
qa.e: They called him 'so slow', so they laughed because he was slow.

qa.q: Story line: "One hot summer, the ponds dried up." What was the problem in the story?
qa.a: There was no water to drink
qa.e: When the ponds dried up, the deer had no water.

qa.q: Dhruv said, "I found it many summers ago." How did Dhruv know about the hidden spring?
qa.a: He had found it long ago
qa.e: 'Many summers ago' means many years ago. He remembered it from long ago.

qa.q: What is the moral of the fable about Dhruv?
qa.a: Elders are wise, so we should respect them
qa.e: The young deer learnt that the slow old stag was wise.

qa.q: What is a fable?
qa.a: A short story with animals acting like people that teaches a lesson
qa.e: A fable has animal characters who talk and act like people, and it has a moral.

qa.q: In "You are slow, but you are wise," what does 'wise' mean?
qa.a: Having good sense from knowing a lot
qa.e: A wise person makes good choices because of what they know.

qa.q: The young deer said, "We are sorry." How did they feel at the end?
qa.e: They said sorry because they had laughed at Dhruv.

qa.q: A stag is a ___ deer.
qa.e: A stag is a male deer. A female deer is a doe.

qa.q: What is the female of 'lion'?
qa.e: The female of lion is lioness.

qa.q: What is a baby deer called?
qa.e: A baby deer is a fawn.

qa.q: What does the proverb 'Look before you leap' mean?
qa.e: It means we should think before we do something.

qa.q: What does 'Slow and steady wins the race' mean?
qa.a: Working steadily without giving up brings success
qa.e: Keeping going steadily, step by step, helps us reach our goal.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'wise'?
qa.e: A wise person is sensible. The others mean the opposite.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'old'?
qa.e: 'Young' is the opposite of 'old'. The others mean old.

qa.q: What is the female of 'peacock'?
qa.e: The female of peacock is peahen.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'go'?
qa.e: 'Go' is a special verb. Its past tense is 'went'.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'cry'?
qa.e: Cry ends in a consonant + y, so y becomes i: cried.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'stop'?
qa.e: For 'stop', we double the p and add -ed: stopped.

qa.q: Fill in: "Yesterday, Meena ___ a mango." (eat)
qa.e: 'Yesterday' tells us it is the past. The past of eat is ate.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the past tense?
qa.e: 'Walked' tells us the action already happened.

qa.q: What is the past tense of 'think'?
qa.e: 'Think' is a special verb. Its past is 'thought'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Last summer, the young deer ___ sorry to Dhruv." (say)
qa.e: The past tense of 'say' is 'said'.

qa.q: Which word in "Last week, we visited the zoo" is a verb in the past tense?
qa.e: 'Visited' is the action, and -ed shows it is in the past.

qa.q: In which country was Louis Braille born?
qa.e: Louis Braille was born in France.

qa.q: In which year was Louis Braille born?
qa.e: He was born in 1809.

qa.q: Story line: "When he was a small child, an accident hurt his eyes." What happened to Louis because of the accident?
qa.e: The accident hurt his eyes, so he could not see.

qa.q: Story line: "He found very few books he could read." What was the problem at his school?
qa.a: There were very few books blind students could read
qa.e: Blind students had very few books they could read.

qa.q: About how old was Louis Braille when he made his dot system?
qa.e: He made it as a teenager, at about fifteen.

qa.q: What is braille made of?
qa.e: Braille is a pattern of raised dots that can be felt.

qa.q: When is World Braille Day?
qa.e: World Braille Day is on 4 January, Louis Braille's birthday.

qa.q: Which word best describes Louis Braille?
qa.e: He did not give up and found a clever new way to read.

qa.q: How many dot places are there in one braille cell?
qa.e: A braille cell has 2 columns of 3, so 6 dot places.

qa.q: How is braille read?
qa.a: By touching the dots with the fingertips
qa.e: Braille is read by touch.

qa.q: In which direction do we read braille?
qa.e: Braille is read from left to right.

qa.q: How is the letter 'a' made in braille?
qa.a: One raised dot at the top left
qa.e: The braille letter 'a' is a single dot at the top left.

qa.q: Which is true about braille?
qa.a: It is a code for reading and writing
qa.e: Braille is a code that can be used for many languages.

qa.q: What is Bharati Braille used for?
qa.e: Bharati Braille is the braille used for Indian languages.

qa.q: Which word means 'standing up above the surface', like braille dots?
qa.e: Braille dots are raised so that they can be felt.

qa.q: Where might you find braille dots?
qa.e: Many lift buttons have braille so that blind people can use them.

qa.q: What does 'inclusion' mean?
qa.a: Making sure everyone can take part
qa.e: Inclusion means no one is left out.

qa.q: Which of these helps a person in a wheelchair enter a building?
qa.e: A ramp is a slope that a wheelchair can roll up.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'kind'?
qa.e: un + kind = unkind, which means not kind.

qa.q: Which word means 'not possible'?
qa.e: We add 'im-' to 'possible' to make 'impossible'.

qa.q: Which word means 'not agree'?
qa.e: dis + agree = disagree.

qa.q: A new girl in class uses a wheelchair. What is the kind thing to do?
qa.a: Invite her to join your group
qa.e: Inviting her makes her feel welcome. That is inclusion.

qa.q: Which is a respectful way to describe someone who cannot see?
qa.a: A person who is visually impaired
qa.e: We use respectful words that describe without hurting.

qa.q: In 'unhappy', which part is the prefix?
qa.e: The prefix 'un-' comes at the start and means 'not'.

qa.q: Story line: "Anaya and her grandfather do yoga on the terrace in Pune." Where do they do yoga?
qa.e: The story says they do yoga on the terrace.

qa.q: Story line: "First they stand tall like a mountain in Tadasana." Tadasana is called the ___ pose.
qa.e: In Tadasana you stand tall and still like a mountain.

qa.q: Which pose needs you to balance on one leg like a tree?
qa.e: In Vrikshasana, the tree pose, you balance on one leg.

qa.q: On which date is International Day of Yoga celebrated?
qa.e: International Day of Yoga is on 21 June every year.

qa.q: Anaya says, "Now my body feels strong and my mind feels calm." How does she feel after yoga?
qa.e: She says her body feels strong and her mind feels calm.

qa.q: Which of these keeps a child fit?
qa.e: Skipping makes the body move and keeps it strong.

qa.q: Bhujangasana is named after which animal?
qa.e: Bhujangasana is the cobra pose. You lift your chest like a cobra raising its head.

qa.q: In 'Fit Nation', what does 'nation' mean?
qa.e: A nation is a country and all the people who live in it.

qa.q: Which of these is a healthy habit?
qa.e: Washing hands removes germs before we eat.

qa.q: How often should we brush our teeth?
qa.e: We should brush our teeth twice a day, in the morning and at night.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'careful'?
qa.e: -ful means 'full of' and -less means 'without'. Careful and careless are opposites.

qa.q: What does 'helpful' mean?
qa.e: Help + ful means full of help, so a helpful person is ready to help.

qa.q: What does 'harmless' mean?
qa.e: -less means 'without', so harmless means without harm.

qa.q: Choose the correct spelling: "Drinking clean water is ___ for our health."
qa.e: The suffix is spelt '-ful' with one l: useful.

qa.q: Which is the healthiest snack?
qa.e: Fruits like bananas give us energy and goodness.

qa.q: Why should we wash our hands with soap?
qa.e: Soap and water wash away germs that can make us ill.

qa.q: Find the adverb: "Anaya stretches slowly."
qa.e: 'Slowly' tells how Anaya stretches.

qa.q: Fill in: "The cheetah runs ___."
qa.e: We need a word that tells how it runs: quickly.

qa.q: Which word tells HOW in "Grandpa lifts the baby gently"?
qa.e: 'Gently' tells how Grandpa lifts the baby.

qa.q: Which is the correct adverb made from 'happy'?
qa.e: Change y to i and add -ly: happily.

qa.q: Fill in: "Please speak ___ in the library."
qa.e: We speak softly in a library so others can read.

qa.q: Which of these words is an adverb?
qa.e: 'Carefully' tells how an action is done.

qa.q: Which word tells WHEN in "We will go to the park tomorrow"?
qa.e: 'Tomorrow' tells when we will go.

qa.q: Which word tells WHERE in "The children are playing outside"?
qa.e: 'Outside' tells where the children are playing.

qa.q: What do you need to play lagori?
qa.a: A ball and a pile of flat stones
qa.e: Lagori is played with a ball and flat stones.

qa.q: Story line: "Team Sunflower threw the ball and knocked down the pile of seven flat stones." How many stones were in the pile?
qa.e: The story says there were seven flat stones.

qa.q: Story line: "Quickly, they began to stack the stones again." What did Team Sunflower do after the pile fell?
qa.e: They began to stack (pile up) the stones again.

qa.q: Story line: "Team Mango tried to get them out with the ball." What did Team Mango try to do?
qa.a: Get the other team out with the ball
qa.e: Team Mango used the ball to try to get Team Sunflower players out.

qa.q: Story line: "Leela placed the last stone and shouted, 'Lagori!'" Why did Leela shout?
qa.a: She had finished building the pile
qa.e: She placed the last stone, so the pile was built again.

qa.q: In many parts of India, lagori is also called ___.
qa.e: Lagori is often called pitthu. Kabaddi, kho-kho and chess are different games.

qa.q: What kind of game is lagori?
qa.e: Lagori has been played in India for a very long time.

qa.q: Which skills help a team win at lagori?
qa.e: You must aim the ball well and work together to build the pile.

qa.q: Team Mango lost but said, "Well played!" What does this show?
qa.e: Praising the winners after losing shows good sportsmanship.

qa.q: What does 'opponent' mean?
qa.a: The person or team you play against
qa.e: Your opponent is on the other side.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'win'?
qa.e: The opposite of win is lose.

qa.q: Which of these is fair play?
qa.e: Fair play means following the rules of the game.

qa.q: What is a champion?
qa.e: A champion is the winner.

qa.q: A player from the other team falls down. What should a good sport do?
qa.e: A good sport cares about every player, even opponents.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'cheer'?
qa.e: To cheer is to shout to encourage someone.

qa.q: Your team lost a match. Which sentence shows you are a good loser?
qa.e: Congratulating the winners is what a good sport does.

qa.q: Which word is a conjunction?
qa.e: 'And' is a joining word.

qa.q: Fill in: "Leela was tired, ___ she kept playing."
qa.e: Being tired and still playing are different ideas, so we use 'but'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Shall we play lagori ___ kabaddi?"
qa.e: We are choosing between two games, so we use 'or'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Raju missed the bus ___ he woke up late."
qa.e: Waking up late is the reason, so we use 'because'.

qa.q: Fill in: "It was raining, ___ we played indoors."
qa.e: Playing indoors is the result of the rain, so we use 'so'.

qa.q: Join the sentences: "Meena has a ball. Meena has a bat."
qa.a: Meena has a ball and a bat.
qa.e: We are adding two things, so we use 'and'.

qa.q: Which conjunction gives a reason?
qa.e: 'Because' tells us why something happened.

qa.q: Fill in: "Our team played well, ___ we did not win."
qa.e: Playing well and not winning are different, so we use 'but'.

qa.q: Passage line: "Tara sat quietly under a neem tree." Where did Tara sit?
qa.e: The passage says she sat under a neem tree.

qa.q: Passage line: "She watched a line of ants carrying tiny crumbs." What were the ants carrying?
qa.e: The ants were carrying tiny crumbs.

qa.q: Passage line: "She heard a bulbul singing on a branch." Which bird did Tara hear?
qa.e: The passage names the bird: a bulbul.

qa.q: Passage line: "She smelt the wet earth after the rain." What did Tara smell?
qa.e: She smelt the wet earth after the rain.

qa.q: Passage line: "A small snail was moving slowly on a leaf." How was the snail moving?
qa.e: The word 'slowly' tells us how the snail moved.

qa.q: Tara thought, "If I sit still and look closely, nature shows me so much!" What did she learn?
qa.a: Looking closely helps us notice many things
qa.e: Sitting still and looking closely helped her see many things.

qa.q: Passage line: "Early one morning, Tara sat quietly under a neem tree." When did Tara sit there?
qa.e: 'Early one morning' tells us the time.

qa.q: In "Tara sat quietly," which word tells how she sat?
qa.e: 'Quietly' tells how she sat.

qa.q: What does 'observation' mean?
qa.e: Observation means noticing things carefully with your senses.

qa.q: Which sense organ helps us hear?
qa.e: We hear with our ears.

qa.q: Which word describes how something feels when you touch it?
qa.e: 'Rough' tells how a surface feels, like tree bark.

qa.q: Which word describes a taste?
qa.e: 'Sour' is a taste, like a raw mango or lemon.

qa.q: Fill in: "I can ___ the birds singing."
qa.e: 'Hear' means to listen with your ears.

qa.q: Fill in: "We swam in the ___ at Puri beach."
qa.e: 'Sea' is the big body of salty water.

qa.q: Which pair of words are homophones?
qa.e: 'Write' and 'right' sound the same but mean different things.

qa.q: Why does Kiran look at a leaf through a magnifying glass?
qa.a: To see its small details clearly
qa.e: A magnifying glass makes small things look bigger so we can observe them.

qa.q: Which word is a preposition?
qa.e: 'Under' tells us position.

qa.q: Fill in: "The cat is hiding ___ the sofa."
qa.e: 'Behind' means at the back of. The cat is at the back of the sofa.

qa.q: Fill in: "The fish swims ___ the water."
qa.e: A fish swims inside the water, so we use 'in'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Riya sat ___ her two friends."
qa.e: She is in the middle of two friends, so we use 'between'.

qa.q: Fill in: "The bird's nest is high ___ the ground."
qa.e: The nest is higher than the ground, so we use 'above'.

qa.q: Which is the preposition in "The bulbul sat on the branch"?
qa.e: 'On' tells us where the bulbul sat.

qa.q: Fill in: "Please put the books ___ the bag."
qa.e: The books go inside the bag, so we use 'in'.

qa.q: What does 'in front of' mean?
qa.e: 'In front of' means ahead of something, at its front side. 'Behind' is its opposite.

qa.q: Poem line: "Under the banyan, my swing hangs low," Where does the swing hang?
qa.e: The line says the swing hangs under the banyan.

qa.q: Poem line: "Didi gives a push and away I go!" Who pushes the swing?
qa.e: The line says Didi gives a push.

qa.q: Poem line: "Forward I fly with my toes to the sun," In which direction does the child go in this line?
qa.e: The line begins 'Forward I fly'.

qa.q: Poem line: "Back I come laughing, oh, what fun!" How does the child feel?
qa.e: The child is laughing and says 'what fun!'

qa.q: Poem lines: "The parrots cheer and the breezes sing, My heart flies high on my happy swing!" Which word rhymes with 'swing'?
qa.e: 'Sing' and 'swing' both end with '-ing'.

qa.q: Poem line: "The parrots cheer and the breezes sing," Who cheers?
qa.e: The line says 'The parrots cheer'.

qa.q: In a poem, one row of words is called a ___.
qa.e: Each row of words in a poem is a line.

qa.q: What is a group of lines in a poem called?
qa.e: A group of lines in a poem is a stanza. A paragraph is used in stories, not poems.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'happy'?
qa.e: 'Joyful' is a synonym of 'happy'.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'push'?
qa.e: We push to move something away and pull to bring it towards us.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'high'?
qa.e: 'Low' is the opposite of 'high'.

qa.q: "Riya could not wait for her turn on the swing." How did Riya feel?
qa.e: 'Could not wait' shows she was excited.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'forward'?
qa.e: 'Backward' is the opposite of 'forward'.

qa.q: Why is outdoor play good for children?
qa.a: It keeps us healthy and happy
qa.e: Running, swinging and playing make our body strong and our mind happy.

qa.q: Children are taking turns on the swing. What does this show?
qa.e: Taking turns is fair and lets everyone play.

qa.q: Which word means 'very happy and excited'?
qa.e: Thrilled means very happy and excited.

qa.q: Fill in: "Didi pushed the swing. ___ pushed it high."
qa.e: Didi is a girl, so we use 'She'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Arjun and I went to the park. ___ played on the swing."
qa.e: Arjun and I together are 'we'.

qa.q: Fill in: "Please give the ball to ___."
qa.e: After 'to' we use 'me', not 'I'.

qa.q: Which word is a pronoun?
qa.e: 'They' takes the place of a noun.

qa.q: Fill in: "The parrots cheered. ___ were happy."
qa.e: Parrots are many, so we use 'They'.

qa.q: Which sentence is correct?
qa.e: The doers of the action take 'I', so we say 'Mohan and I went home.'

qa.q: Fill in: "Grandpa called Ravi and Asha. He gave ___ some laddoos."
qa.e: Ravi and Asha receive the laddoos, so after the verb we use 'them'.

qa.q: Which pronoun is always written with a capital letter?
qa.e: The pronoun 'I' is always a capital letter.

qa.q: Story line: "Ishaan's family took the toy train from Kalka to Shimla." How did they travel?
qa.e: They took the toy train.

qa.q: Story line: "The little train puffed through tunnels and over bridges." What did the train go through?
qa.e: The train went through tunnels and over bridges.

qa.q: Story line: "Pine trees stood tall on the slopes." Which trees grew on the slopes?
qa.e: The story names pine trees.

qa.q: Story line: "Far away, Ishaan saw snowy peaks shining in the sun." What did Ishaan see far away?
qa.e: He saw snowy mountain peaks.

qa.q: "The mountains look magical!" he gasped. How did Ishaan feel?
qa.e: 'Gasped' and 'magical' show he was amazed.

qa.q: Story line: "That night, it was so cold that he slept under two warm quilts." Why did he use two quilts?
qa.e: The night was so cold that he needed two quilts.

qa.q: Story line: "In May, Ishaan's family took the toy train." In which month was the trip?
qa.e: The story begins 'In May'.

qa.q: What is a travel story about?
qa.e: A travel story tells about a journey and what people saw.

qa.q: What is the top of a mountain called?
qa.e: The highest point of a mountain is its peak.

qa.q: What do we call low land between hills or mountains?
qa.e: A valley is low land between hills or mountains.

qa.q: What is a glacier?
qa.a: A huge mass of ice that moves slowly
qa.e: A glacier is a huge mass of ice that moves very slowly.

qa.q: What is high, flat land called?
qa.e: A plateau is high and flat. A plain is flat but low.

qa.q: Which is the highest mountain in the world?
qa.e: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

qa.q: Which great mountain range is in the north of India?
qa.e: The Himalayas stretch across the north of India.

qa.q: What is land with water all around it called?
qa.e: An island has water on all sides.

qa.q: Most of India's Thar Desert is in which state?
qa.e: Most of the Thar Desert lies in Rajasthan.

qa.q: Fill in: "This hill is ___ than that one." (big)
qa.e: Comparing two things: big → bigger (double the g).

qa.q: Fill in: "Of the three peaks, this one is the ___." (tall)
qa.e: Comparing three or more: tallest.

qa.q: Which word compares two things using 'good'?
qa.e: good → better → best. 'Better' compares two.

qa.q: Fill in: "The valley is ___ than the town." (beautiful)
qa.e: Long words use 'more' to compare two things.

qa.q: Which word means 'the most bad'?
qa.e: bad → worse → worst.

qa.q: Fill in: "Today is ___ than yesterday." (cold)
qa.e: Comparing two days: colder.

qa.q: Fill in: "Ishaan was the ___ child on the train." (happy)
qa.e: Comparing him with all the children: change y to i and add -est.

qa.q: Fill in: "A glacier moves ___ than a river." (slow)
qa.e: Comparing two things, so we add -er: slower.

qa.q: In which state is Maheshwar?
qa.e: Maheshwar is in Madhya Pradesh.

qa.q: Maheshwar is on the banks of which river?
qa.e: Maheshwar is on the Narmada.

qa.q: Passage line: "Long stone steps called ghats lead down to the water." What are ghats?
qa.a: Steps leading down to the river
qa.e: The line tells us ghats are stone steps that lead to the water.

qa.q: Passage line: "Above the ghats stands the old Ahilya Fort." What stands above the ghats?
qa.e: The passage says the Ahilya Fort stands above the ghats.

qa.q: Which queen made Maheshwar her capital?
qa.e: Rani Ahilyabai Holkar ruled from Maheshwar. The fort is named after her.

qa.q: Passage line: "You can hear the clack-clack of handlooms." Which is the sound word?
qa.e: 'Clack-clack' copies the sound a loom makes.

qa.q: Into which sea does the Narmada flow?
qa.e: The Narmada flows west and falls into the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: In "on the banks of the river", what does 'banks' mean?
qa.a: The land along the sides of a river
qa.e: 'Bank' has more than one meaning. Next to a river, it means the land at its side.

qa.q: What is a handloom?
qa.e: A handloom is worked by the weaver's hands and feet, without electricity.

qa.q: Maheshwari sarees are made in which town?
qa.e: They are named after the town of Maheshwar.

qa.q: What does 'heritage' mean?
qa.a: Things from the past that we value and pass on
qa.e: Heritage is what we get from the past and want to keep for the future.

qa.q: A person who weaves cloth is called a ___.
qa.e: A weaver makes cloth. A tailor stitches clothes from cloth.

qa.q: Which tool carries the weft thread across the loom?
qa.e: The shuttle moves across the loom carrying the weft thread.

qa.q: When is National Handloom Day?
qa.e: National Handloom Day is on 7 August.

qa.q: Why should we support handloom crafts?
qa.a: They are part of our heritage and give weavers work
qa.e: Buying handloom keeps the old craft alive and helps weavers earn.

qa.q: Which of these words is made by joining two smaller words?
qa.e: hand + loom = handloom.

qa.q: In "We took a boat on the narmada.", which word needs a capital letter?
qa.e: Narmada is the name of a river, so it needs a capital N.

qa.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly?
qa.a: We bought cotton, silk and thread.
qa.e: Commas go between the items of a list: cotton, silk and thread.

qa.q: Which of these words should always begin with a capital letter?
qa.e: Days of the week are special names, so they always need a capital letter.

qa.q: Where should the comma go? "Yes I would like to visit Maheshwar."
qa.e: We put a comma after 'Yes' at the start: Yes, I would like to visit Maheshwar.

qa.q: Why does 'Ahilyabai' begin with a capital letter?
qa.a: It is the name of a person
qa.e: Names of people are proper nouns and need a capital letter.

qa.q: Which list is written correctly?
qa.e: We put a comma between list items, and 'and' before the last one.

qa.q: Which word does NOT need a capital letter in the middle of a sentence?
qa.e: Seasons like winter are not special names, so they do not need a capital letter.

qa.q: Find the mistake: "My friend ravi lives in Indore."
qa.e: Ravi is a person's name, so it needs a capital R.
